lessons_that_transfer: First prove how the maps were made: fit brightness recipe + straight stretch (two cut-off numbers) + blur + normal strength from reference colour to reference height/normal (wood: 0.299R+0.587G+0.114B, (b-12)/116, blur 0.5, normal strength 8: height 4.15 steps, normal 4.3 degrees). Then height and normal come from the finished colour inside the generator and only the colour must be described.

Count the same-colour areas by size class before designing anything (wood: 92,000 areas, equal area share in every doubling class from 4 to 2000 dots). It tells you the traced description will be hundreds of KB and the fine detail can only be invented.

Trace by joining the two neighbouring patches that differ least (Ward clustering) and colouring each patch with its average colour: SSIM 0.76 against 0.53 at 600 KB for 'drop small areas'. Make outline looseness follow patch thickness, or 400 patches still cost 139 KB. Let patches join across the tile edge so a patch keeps one colour there.

One generator for every flat painted surface: every element becomes a flat coloured polygon, drawn back to front as one Blender mesh (each shape a hair above the last, camera above all), photographed from above with Cycles; polygons touching the tile edge are redrawn shifted +-1 tile; the fine structure comes from a shader node group (seamless stretched noise cut at two levels).

Invented paint must be colour-relative: cover the board with slowly varying zones (colour from three slow fields with fitted mean/spread), then strips whose colour = colour beneath + small fitted change. A plain colour probability table gives camouflage confetti.

What each layer buys: layout buys structure, invented paint plus grain buys the 'same kind' look (0.21 -> 0.63 for 6 KB) but costs dot-for-dot accuracy; tracing buys the match (SSIM 0.42 at 24 KB, 0.59 at 150 KB, 0.72 at 462 KB). Grain on top of tracing raises same-kind (0.46 -> 0.76) but lowers SSIM (0.67 -> 0.51).
Keep sampler seeds for EVERY random part (including grain noise seeds) or all tiles share fine detail; keep palette jitter to lightness/warmth shifts so tiles are not tinted.

Test seamlessness by baking the pattern shifted by half a tile (including any position-fixed shader grain) and comparing with the first picture rolled by half; compare a wrong roll as control; measure edge jumps in the same direction as the jump (along rows for vertical edges, down columns for horizontal edges).

Normal angle is the measure that costs most bytes for fine-grained surfaces (flat normal 24 degrees off; 300 KB trace 16.8; 470 KB trace 15.5; earlier 1.5 MB test 12.6): do not expect the 'close' tier at 512 KB and do not chase it with random grain.

Transfer by changing numbers and a few hand-written lists only; write down what changed. Waiting scripts must wait on a file or line count, never search for their own name (pkill/pgrep -f killed my own shell twice).

derivation_ceiling: Reference height = brightness (0.299R+0.587G+0.114B of the picture's own numbers), straight stretch (b-12)/116 cut at 0..1, blur 0.5 dots: mean error 4.15 steps of 255 (free 64-point tone curve 4.06), correlation 0.9946. Reference normal = slope of the 8-bit height (left/right dot difference /2) x strength 8: 0.34 degrees from the uploaded height; 4.3 degrees through the colour-derived height; a flat normal is 24.1 degrees off. So with a perfect colour the maps would be wrong by about 4 steps and 4 degrees.
geometry_route_verdict: Tried: cracks as Blender Curve objects (poly curve, bevel, point radius = half width so the taper is automatic) and splatter blobs by Geometry Nodes (points with radius and colour -> Instance on Points with a circle -> Realize Instances -> Set Material), planks stay polygons. Same sampled description (seed 5, 200 cracks, 458 blobs) vs the numpy-polygon route: mean difference 0.134 brightness steps, 0.10 % of dots differ by more than 40 (nodes give perfect circles, polygons ragged ones); time 11.6 s against 15.3 s. Verdict: identical picture; taper is one setting and scatter is one node tree (real advantages), but one object per crack does not scale to thousands of traced patches and paint edges need extra noise nodes. For flat painted surfaces the polygon painter is simpler and as good; geometry would pay for real relief (grooves, raised splinters), which was not tested.
